Understanding Java Virtual Threads: A Practical Guide

Java 21 introduced virtual threads as a stable feature (JEP 444), fundamentally changing how we write concurrent applications. In this post, we'll explore what virtual threads are, why they matter, and how to use them effectively.

What Are Virtual Threads?

Traditional Java threads (platform threads) are thin wrappers around operating system threads. They're expensive to create and limited in number—typically a few thousand before you exhaust system resources.

Virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. You can create millions of them without breaking a sweat, making them ideal for high-throughput concurrent applications.

The Problem They Solve

Before virtual threads, the standard approach to high concurrency was reactive programming or thread pools. Consider a typical blocking I/O scenario:

java
// Platform thread approach - limited scalability
try (var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200)) {
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
executor.submit(() -> {
// Blocking call ties up a precious OS thread
return fetchDataFromDatabase();
});
}
}

With only 200 threads, requests queue up when all threads are blocked on I/O.

Using Virtual Threads

The API is refreshingly simple. Here's the same logic with virtual threads:

java
// Virtual thread approach - massive scalability
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
executor.submit(() -> {
// Blocking here is cheap - JVM unmounts the virtual thread
return fetchDataFromDatabase();
});
}
}

You can also create them directly:

java
Thread vThread = Thread.ofVirtual()
.name("worker-", 0)
.start(() -> System.out.println("Running in " + Thread.currentThread()));

vThread.join();

How It Works Under the Hood

When a virtual thread hits a blocking operation, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread and mounts another virtual thread. This means blocking code no longer blocks OS threads—you write simple, synchronous code that scales like asynchronous code.

java
// This blocking code is now efficient with virtual threads
String result = httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
processResult(result);

Best Practices

  1. Don't pool virtual threads — create a new one per task. They're cheap.
  2. Avoid synchronized blocks for long I/O operations; they can pin a virtual thread to its carrier. Prefer ReentrantLock.
  3. Use them for I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound tasks where platform threads still shine.

java
// Prefer ReentrantLock over synchronized to avoid pinning
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void safeOperation() {
lock.lock();
try {
performIO();
} finally {
lock.unlock();
}
}

Spring Boot Integration

Spring Boot 3.2+ supports virtual threads with a single property:

properties
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

This configures Tomcat and other executors to use virtual threads automatically, boosting throughput for typical web applications with minimal effort.

Conclusion

Virtual threads let you write straightforward, blocking-style code that scales to millions of concurrent operations. They eliminate much of the complexity of reactive programming while delivering comparable performance for I/O-bound workloads. If you're on Java 21 or later, they're worth adopting today.
